analysis.one_liner: Requires a seven-day waiting period and police background check before handgun sales.
analysis.headline: The Senate Brady bill never left committee; a version of the same idea became federal law in November 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for licensed gun dealers to hand over a handgun until a local police chief or sheriff had up to seven days to check whether the buyer is legally barred from having one — a felony record, fugitive status, drug addiction, certain mental-health commitments, or illegal presence in the country. Buyers with permits, or in states that already run their own checks or waiting periods, would be exempt. Records of legal purchases would have to be destroyed within 30 days.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk from gun violence. The waiting period gives local law enforcement time to check a buyer's background before the sale goes through, and buyers facing a documented threat to themselves or their family could get a handgun immediately.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: A licensed dealer could not complete a handgun sale until a chief law enforcement officer had up to seven days to review the buyer's sworn statement and report any legal bar to possession, or confirm there is none.

The buyer's statement must attest they are not under indictment or convicted of a serious crime, not a fugitive, not an unlawful drug user, not subject to certain mental-health adjudications, not unlawfully in the country, and not dishonorably discharged or a renounced citizen.
The bill protects buyers' privacy: unless a check turns up a legal problem, the officer must destroy the buyer's statement and any records derived from it within 30 days.

Someone who presents a police statement that they or a family member face a specific threat can bypass the waiting period, and buyers in states with their own permit-and-verification systems are exempt.

analysis.who_pays: Handgun buyers would wait up to seven days for their purchase. Licensed dealers would keep signed statements on file and risk fines up to $1,000 and a year in jail for violations. Local police chiefs and sheriffs would do the checks without any new funding written into the bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun buyers, dealers, and local police

drawbacks.text: The waiting period delays every handgun purchase through a licensed dealer, including by buyers with no disqualifying record, and the bill gives local police this new workload with no dedicated funding.
The requirement applies only to licensed dealers and manufacturers, so private, unlicensed transfers are untouched — a gap that limits how much the waiting period can do.

Supporters of unrestricted sales argued a delay burdens law-abiding buyers; the bill's answer was its threat exemption and its short-list of disqualifying conditions, but the seven-day wait still applies broadly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is real but modest: a delay of days for buyers and extra paperwork for dealers and police. The benefit is that police get a window to catch legally prohibited buyers before a sale. The biggest design weakness is that private sales fall outside the law entirely, so the check only covers the licensed market.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and its Constitution subcommittee for two years and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act on January 23, 1991, joined at introduction by eleven other senators including Republicans Nancy Kassebaum and John Chafee.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and on February 20, 1991 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution.
No committee, subcommittee, or floor action followed; the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993 with the bill still in committee.
Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill — fourteen Democrats and two Republicans.
Two years later, in the next Congress, the Brady Act passed and was signed into law in November 1993, establishing the waiting-period background check this bill proposed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of a national waiting period kept the requirement off the books for two more years, though Congress enacted a version of it in the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun-check opponents, for two more years

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eleven original cosponsors across both parties.

for.name: Nancy Kassebaum
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from day one.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, sent it to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, and never reported it out during the two-year Congress.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained public campaign against the Brady waiting period through the late 1980s and early 1990s, making it one of the most contested measures in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sixteen senators cosponsored the bill, fourteen Democrats and two Republicans, and no votes were ever held on it.

industries.note: The bill bars them from completing handgun sales until a police check clears the buyer or seven days pass, requires them to keep signed buyer statements on file, and carries fines up to $1,000 and a year in jail for violations. Dealers' interest in fast, unrestricted sales ran against the bill's screening benefit.
The prohibition covers transfers by licensed manufacturers and importers as well as dealers, adding the same waiting-period gate to their handgun transactions.

Police chiefs and sheriffs would gain a formal screening role over handgun sales but would absorb the workload — receiving statements, checking buyers, and destroying records within 30 days — without new funding.
